section: Can technology help when workers are scarce?
text:
Can technology help when workers are scarce?
Total output equals hours worked multiplied by output per hour.
If hours worked fall by 10%, how much must output per hour rise to keep total output steady?

About 11.1%. With 90% of the original hours, output per hour must rise to \(1/0.90\) times its original level.



This is an illustration of the productivity gain needed to offset fewer hours. Ask students what might help firms achieve such a gain.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
The balance of payments
The balance of payments records transactions between residents and nonresidents over a period.

Current account records trade, income, and current transfers.
Capital account records capital transfers and transactions in certain nonfinancial assets.
Financial account records transactions in external financial assets and liabilities.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Current account

Goods — a Japanese firm exports machinery or imports fuel.
Services — a visitor from abroad pays for a hotel in Japan. Japan records a service export.
Primary income — a Japanese investor receives dividends on shares in a foreign company.
Secondary income — a resident of Japan sends money as a gift to family living abroad.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Capital account

Capital transfers include debt forgiveness. If Japan’s government forgives a loan owed by a foreign government, Japan records a capital transfer paid and a reduction in its external loan assets.
Nonproduced nonfinancial assets include certain rights. A Japanese company buying ownership of an existing trademark from a nonresident records the acquisition here.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Financial account

External assets are financial claims that residents hold on nonresidents. A Japanese resident buying a foreign bond increases Japan’s external assets.
External liabilities are financial claims that nonresidents hold on residents. A foreign investor buying a newly issued Japanese government bond increases Japan’s external liabilities.
Reserve assets are external assets held by the monetary authorities. They are part of the financial account.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Sign convention: net lending (IMF BPM6)


Current and capital account: the balance is credits minus debits. Exports are credits and imports are debits
Financial account: an increase in assets is +, an increase in liabilities is + in the liabilities column, and net lending = change in assets - change in liabilities
So a surplus in CA + KA is matched by a positive financial account balance: the country is a net lender
Older textbooks (BPM5 style) record asset increases as debits, so the financial account has the opposite sign and the three accounts sum to zero

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
section: Why does Japan run surpluses? Saving and investment
text:
Why does Japan run surpluses? Saving and investment
\[ CA = S - I \]


\(S\): national saving, \(I\): domestic investment
A CA surplus means the country saves more than it invests at home, and the excess contributes to net lending abroad
So the CA is a macro outcome, not only a trade outcome: high household and corporate saving relative to domestic investment opportunities




This is the link to the last lesson: aging changes S, so it changes the CA.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
section: Reserve assets: the official part of the financial account
text:
Reserve assets: the official part of the financial account


Reserve assets are foreign assets held by the authorities (MOF decides, the BOJ acts as agent)
When the authorities buy dollars and sell yen to influence the exchange rate, reserve assets rise: this is a financial account entry
Unlike private flows, reserve changes are a policy decision




Details of intervention (why, when, sterilization, accords) are in the exchange rate lesson.

text:
Japan’s NIIP











Level Japan has one of the world’s largest positive NIIPs (~US$3–4 trillion, >80% of GDP 2024).
Reflects decades of current account surpluses and outward FDI. (US: -90% of its nominal GDP 2024)
Resilience Stable external position despite aging and yen fluctuations.
Suggests strong net creditor status and global financial reach.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Japan as a mature creditor

A stylized path:

Growth era: current account roughly balanced, limited by foreign reserves
Trade-surplus era: goods surplus drives the CA; outward FDI and portfolio investment build external assets
Mature creditor: returns on those assets (primary income) rival or exceed the goods balance; the CA stays in surplus even when goods trade is in deficit (e.g., 2011, 2022)




The current account components chart shows how primary income offsets the goods deficit.
Japan’s external position is now sustained by the return on past saving, not only by exports.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Valuation and the yen

Toy example:

Japan holds US$1 trillion of foreign assets and has no foreign-currency liabilities
At ¥100/$: assets = ¥100 trillion
At ¥150/$: assets = ¥150 trillion
+¥50 trillion in the yen value of NIIP, with no transaction at all



Much of Japan’s external assets are in foreign currency, while a larger share of its liabilities is in yen, so a weaker yen tends to raise NIIP measured in yen



In dollar terms nothing changed: say that explicitly, because NIIP is reported in different currencies in different sources (USD in the OECD chart, yen in MOF data).
Link to 2022: the yen’s depreciation raised the yen value of foreign assets while making imports more expensive. The same exchange rate move hits the two sides of the balance sheet and the trade balance in opposite directions.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
The balance of payments
The balance of payments records transactions between residents and nonresidents over a period.

Current account records trade, income, and current transfers.
Capital account records capital transfers and transactions in certain nonfinancial assets.
Financial account records transactions in external financial assets and liabilities.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Current account

Goods — a Japanese firm exports machinery or imports fuel.
Services — a visitor from abroad pays for a hotel in Japan. Japan records a service export.
Primary income — a Japanese investor receives dividends on shares in a foreign company.
Secondary income — a resident of Japan sends money as a gift to family living abroad.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Capital account

Capital transfers include debt forgiveness. If Japan’s government forgives a loan owed by a foreign government, Japan records a capital transfer paid and a reduction in its external loan assets.
Nonproduced nonfinancial assets include certain rights. A Japanese company buying ownership of an existing trademark from a nonresident records the acquisition here.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Financial account

External assets are financial claims that residents hold on nonresidents. A Japanese resident buying a foreign bond increases Japan’s external assets.
External liabilities are financial claims that nonresidents hold on residents. A foreign investor buying a newly issued Japanese government bond increases Japan’s external liabilities.
Reserve assets are external assets held by the monetary authorities. They are part of the financial account.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Sign convention: net lending (IMF BPM6)

Current and capital account: the balance is credits minus debits. Exports are credits and imports are debits
Financial account: an increase in assets is +, an increase in liabilities is + in the liabilities column, and net lending = change in assets - change in liabilities
So a surplus in CA + KA is matched by a positive financial account balance: the country is a net lender
Older textbooks (BPM5 style) record asset increases as debits, so the financial account has the opposite sign and the three accounts sum to zero

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
section: Why does Japan run surpluses? Saving and investment
text:
Why does Japan run surpluses? Saving and investment
\[ CA = S - I \]

\(S\): national saving, \(I\): domestic investment
A CA surplus means the country saves more than it invests at home, and the excess contributes to net lending abroad
So the CA is a macro outcome, not only a trade outcome: high household and corporate saving relative to domestic investment opportunities



This is the link to the last lesson: aging changes S, so it changes the CA.

text:
Reserve assets: the official part of the financial account

Reserve assets are foreign assets held by the authorities (MOF decides, the BOJ acts as agent)
When the authorities buy dollars and sell yen to influence the exchange rate, reserve assets rise: this is a financial account entry
Unlike private flows, reserve changes are a policy decision



Details of intervention (why, when, sterilization, accords) are in the exchange rate lesson.

Japan’s NIIP



Level Japan has one of the world’s largest positive NIIPs (~US$3–4 trillion, >80% of GDP 2024).
Reflects decades of current account surpluses and outward FDI. (US: -90% of its nominal GDP 2024)
Resilience Stable external position despite aging and yen fluctuations.

title: Balance of Payments: Accounts and Japan’s External Position
text:
Japan as a mature creditor
A stylized path:

Growth era: current account roughly balanced, limited by foreign reserves
Trade-surplus era: goods surplus drives the CA; outward FDI and portfolio investment build external assets
Mature creditor: returns on those assets (primary income) rival or exceed the goods balance; the CA stays in surplus even when goods trade is in deficit (e.g., 2011, 2022)



The current account components chart shows how primary income offsets the goods deficit.
Japan’s external position is now sustained by the return on past saving, not only by exports.

text:
Valuation and the yen
Toy example:

Japan holds US$1 trillion of foreign assets and has no foreign-currency liabilities
At ¥100/$: assets = ¥100 trillion
At ¥150/$: assets = ¥150 trillion
+¥50 trillion in the yen value of NIIP, with no transaction at all


Much of Japan’s external assets are in foreign currency, while a larger share of its liabilities is in yen, so a weaker yen tends to raise NIIP measured in yen



In dollar terms nothing changed: say that explicitly, because NIIP is reported in different currencies in different sources (USD in the OECD chart, yen in MOF data).
Link to 2022: the yen’s depreciation raised the yen value of foreign assets while making imports more expensive. The same exchange rate move hits the two sides of the balance sheet and the trade balance in opposite directions.

text:
Japan as aid recipients


1946 ~ 1951, Japan received a total of USD5 billion in US aid (financed 40% Japanese imports)

Part of the repayment for the US was used to finance US-Japan cultural exchange (including the Fullbright program)

1953 ~ 1966, the World Bank provided USD860 million for 34 development projects in the country: Tanagawa Dam, Tokaido Bullet Train (from Tokyo to Osaka), the Tōmei Highway (from Tokyo to Nagoya), and the Kurobe hydroelectric dam

text:

Japan joined DAG in 1960, became founding member of OECD-DAC in 1961
Japan joined Colombo Plan in 1954,

Started paying reparations to other Asian countries until 1976 (central aspects of Japan’s economic foreign policy toward Asian countries until mid 1960s)
Began providing technical experts, training, and equipment to Asian countries

Gradually aligned with DAC norms (grant element, untying, evaluation)
Adopted global themes (environment, gender, participation)

humanitarian considerations
recognition of interdependence among nations of the international community
environmental consideration

Debates on ODA effectiveness


In theory, ODA effect can be

Positive: use ODA to invest and grow
Non-positive: use ODA to consume luxury goods

Empirical studies:

Aid has no effect on growth (early 1970 studies)
Aid has a positive relationship with growth on average with diminishing returns (1990s studies)
Aid has a conditional relationship with growth:

Good policies (Burnside and Dollar, 2000)
Climate, institutional quality, political conflict, and geography (Hansen and Tarp, 2001)


Each type of aid has different impact on growth:

Humanitarian aid: no direct impact
Infrastructure aid: positive impact (Easterly, 2003)

title: Official Development Assistance
text:
ODA as infrastructure financing


Japan’s ODA historically supported infrastructure and industrial development in Asia
Loans and technical cooperation, often tied to Japanese firms (“ingredients approach”)
Japan itself was financed this way: World Bank loans built the Tokaido Bullet Train, the Tōmei Highway and the Kurobe dam
Infrastructure aid is the type most consistently linked to growth (Easterly, 2003)

title: Official Development Assistance
text:
Debates on ODA effectiveness


In theory, ODA effect can be

Positive: use ODA to invest and grow
Non-positive: use ODA to consume luxury goods

Empirical studies:

Aid has no effect on growth (early 1970 studies)
Aid has a positive relationship with growth on average with diminishing returns (1990s studies)
Aid has a conditional relationship with growth:

Good policies (Burnside and Dollar, 2000)
Climate, institutional quality, political conflict, and geography (Hansen and Tarp, 2001)


Each type of aid has different impact on growth:

Humanitarian aid: no direct impact
Infrastructure aid: positive impact (Easterly, 2003)

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Trade in Tasks

Traditional trade theory: countries exchange complete, finished goods
Grossman & Rossi-Hansberg (2008): production is unbundled into discrete tasks — design, component sourcing, fabrication, assembly, testing, marketing
Comparative advantage now applies task-by-task, not product-by-product
A task is offshored when it can be performed abroad more cheaply, net of coordination and trade costs



WTO and JETRO-IDE (2011) reframe East Asian trade as evolving “from trade in goods to trade in tasks”
Explains the rise of intra-industry, intra-firm trade in intermediate goods
A country’s export mix reflects which tasks it specializes in, not which whole product it exports

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
The Smile Curve











Introduced by Acer founder and CEO Stan Shih in the early 1990s: - the early and late stages of the supply chains generate higher value added
The share of value added in manufactured products is shifting from the fabrication stages to pre- and post-fabrication services.

reclassification: from in-house to outsourced -> factory-less manufacturer
task-composition shifts: more logistics, transportation, communication to move intermediates or more software/design etc final goods
task–relative price shifts: off-shoring to reduce the relative price of the off-shored tasks.

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Trade in Value Added

Gross trade statistics double-count intermediate inputs that cross borders multiple times before reaching the final consumer
The Trade in Value Added (TiVA) approach reallocates exports to the country that actually created the value:

Domestic Value Added (DVA): value added by the exporting country itself
Foreign Value Added (FVA): value added by other countries, embodied in imported inputs




Gross exports overstate bilateral imbalances (e.g., the US–China trade deficit narrows substantially once measured in value-added terms)
Value-added trade better reflects which country actually benefits from a given trade flow

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
section: Key Features of Global Value Chains
text:
Key Features of Global Value Chains

Fragmentation of Production: across multiple countries for cost structures, labor markets, and expertise
Specialization: specific segments of the chain (R&D, design, manufacturing, logistics )
Interconnection: trade, investment, and technology
Value creation: value added chain from materials to final goods
Global distribution: multiple markets

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Measuring GVC Participation
Backward linkage (backward participation)
\[ \text{Backward} = \frac{FVA}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Forward linkage (forward participation)
\[ \text{Forward} = \frac{DVX}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Total GVC participation = Backward + Forward


Based on the gross export decomposition in Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014), built from international input–output tables
Small, open economies (e.g., ASEAN members) tend to show higher backward participation. They import more of what they need to export
Countries positioned at the start of chains (raw materials, core components, R&D) tend to show higher forward participation
Rule of thumb: Backward ↑ when a country imports a lot of intermediates; Forward ↑ when a country’s intermediates are re-exported by others

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Decompose Gross Trade

Traditional trade: cross border once
GVC-related trade: cross border at least twice

Pure backward participation: the use of foreign inputs in exports to the final destination (chain end)
Pure forward participation: the use of domestically produced intermediates in third-country exports (chain start)
Mixed participation: the use of foreign intermediates in third-country exports

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
GVC intensity and GVC position

How strongly is a country or industry involved in GVC production?

\[
\text{GVC Participation}
=
\text{Pure Backward}
+
\text{Pure Forward}
+
\text{Mixed}
\]

Where does the country or industry tend to operate in the value chain?

\[
Forwardness = \frac{\text{Pure Forward} - \text{Pure Backward}}{\text{Total GVC Participation}}
\]

Summed over all countries, sectors and partners, pure forward activity equals pure backward activity.
At the country-sector level, 0 means pure forward and pure backward are balanced, so the sector is neither mainly at the start nor mainly at the end of chains, relative to the world average. Positive values mean more upstream (supplying inputs), negative values mean more downstream (assembling from imported inputs).
Alternative measures of GVC position include upstreamness (distance of output from final demand) and downstreamness (distance from primary inputs/value added). These measures are conceptually related to, but distinct from, WITS forwardness.

Upstream (high value): design, R&D, core components, precise machinery
Midstream: capital goods exports, management of production networks
Downstream: limited (assembly shifted to China/ASEAN), but could be different for chemicals (pharmaceutical synthesis)

Trade in Tasks

Traditional trade theory: countries exchange complete, finished goods
Grossman & Rossi-Hansberg (2008): production is unbundled into discrete tasks — design, component sourcing, fabrication, assembly, testing, marketing
Comparative advantage now applies task-by-task, not product-by-product
A task is offshored when it can be performed abroad more cheaply, net of coordination and trade costs



WTO and JETRO-IDE (2011) reframe East Asian trade as evolving “from trade in goods to trade in tasks”
Explains the rise of intra-industry, intra-firm trade in intermediate goods
A country’s export mix reflects which tasks it specializes in, not which whole product it exports

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Trade in Value Added

Gross trade statistics double-count intermediate inputs that cross borders multiple times before reaching the final consumer
The Trade in Value Added (TiVA) approach reallocates exports to the country that actually created the value:

Domestic Value Added (DVA): value added by the exporting country itself
Foreign Value Added (FVA): value added by other countries, embodied in imported inputs




Gross exports overstate bilateral imbalances (e.g., the US–China trade deficit narrows substantially once measured in value-added terms)
Value-added trade better reflects which country actually benefits from a given trade flow

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Measuring GVC Participation
Backward linkage (backward participation)
\[ \text{Backward} = \frac{FVA}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Forward linkage (forward participation)
\[ \text{Forward} = \frac{DVX}{\text{Gross Exports}} \times 100 \] Total GVC participation = Backward + Forward


Based on the gross export decomposition in Koopman, Wang & Wei (2014), built from international input–output tables
Small, open economies (e.g., ASEAN members) tend to show higher backward participation. They import more of what they need to export
Countries positioned at the start of chains (raw materials, core components, R&D) tend to show higher forward participation
Rule of thumb: Backward ↑ when a country imports a lot of intermediates; Forward ↑ when a country’s intermediates are re-exported by others

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
Decompose Gross Trade

Traditional trade: cross border once
GVC-related trade: cross border at least twice

Pure backward participation: the use of foreign inputs in exports to the final destination (chain end)
Pure forward participation: the use of domestically produced intermediates in third-country exports (chain start)
Mixed participation: the use of foreign intermediates in third-country exports

title: Measurement of Global Value Chains
text:
GVC intensity and GVC position

How strongly is a country or industry involved in GVC production?

\[
\text{GVC Participation}
=
\text{Pure Backward}
+
\text{Pure Forward}
+
\text{Mixed}
\]

Where does the country or industry tend to operate in the value chain?

\[
Forwardness = \frac{\text{Pure Forward} - \text{Pure Backward}}{\text{Total GVC Participation}}
\]

Summed over all countries, sectors and partners, pure forward activity equals pure backward activity.
At the country-sector level, 0 means pure forward and pure backward are balanced, so the sector is neither mainly at the start nor mainly at the end of chains, relative to the world average. Positive values mean more upstream (supplying inputs), negative values mean more downstream (assembling from imported inputs).
Alternative measures of GVC position include upstreamness (distance of output from final demand) and downstreamness (distance from primary inputs/value added). These measures are conceptually related to, but distinct from, WITS forwardness.

Upstream (high value): design, R&D, core components, precise machinery
Midstream: capital goods exports, management of production networks
Downstream: limited (assembly shifted to China/ASEAN), but could be different for chemicals (pharmaceutical synthesis)

Economic growth comes from two different sources:

More inputs: working more hours, employing more people, building more capital, or having a more educated workforce

Why demographics matter

Growth drivers: labor supply directly feeds into the growth accounting framework
Market size: a country’s population sets the scale of domestic demand
Consumption: a population’s age structure drives spending patterns
Saving: national saving rates (working-age people save for retirement; retirees draw savings down)



Labor was one of the four inputs; this section asks “what happens when that input starts shrinking?”
Japan’s median age is now the highest among peers, with population decline already underway. The next two slides show this directly, plus whether migration is offsetting it.
Aging affects saving in offsetting ways: life-cycle theory predicts lower aggregate saving as retirees dissave, but this is debated empirically for Japan specifically because household saving rates have been unusually resilient.

title: Introduction
text:
Growth accounting: the framework
Economic growth comes from two different sources:

More inputs: working more hours, employing more people, building more capital, or having a more educated workforce
Using inputs better: technology, efficiency, and innovation that let the same inputs produce more output (this is called Total Factor Productivity, or TFP)



Each panel shows the annual growth rate (%) of one input, or of TFP
Japan’s inputs kept growing, but TFP growth stalled
TFP is measured as a residual — growth left over after accounting for capital, labor, and human capital growth

Yen as store of value



This shows only one dimension (store of value / reserve holdings), not trade invoicing or pricing, worth noting the yen may play a bigger or smaller role in other functions
The yen has held a stable, mid-sized share of global reserves for decades, which reflects Japan’s role as a safe-haven currency despite its shrinking share of world GDP

title: Introduction
text:
Why demographics matter

Growth drivers: labor supply directly feeds into the growth accounting framework
Market size: a country’s population sets the scale of domestic demand
Consumption: a population’s age structure drives spending patterns
Saving: national saving rates (working-age people save for retirement; retirees draw savings down)



Labor was one of the four inputs; this section asks “what happens when that input starts shrinking?”
Japan’s median age is now the highest among peers, with population decline already underway. The next two slides show this directly, plus whether migration is offsetting it.
Aging affects saving in offsetting ways: life-cycle theory predicts lower aggregate saving as retirees dissave, but this is debated empirically for Japan specifically because household saving rates have been unusually resilient.

Japan at a glance: takeaways

High-income: Japan converged with advanced economies decades ago, but stalled since the 1990s
Growth model: Initially investment- and export-led, with rising TFP but since the 1990s, all drivers slowed
Safe-haven currency: the yen has held a stable share of global reserves for decades
Aging economy: a shrinking, aging population is now squeezing the labor input directly

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Overview
This document documents the data-cleaning pipeline for the WITS GVC trade dataset. It covers:

Loading the raw trade, sector, and country reference tables
Classifying countries into analytical regions
Merging trade data with sector and region metadata
Reshaping the merged data into long format for downstream analysis

Analysis, plotting, and index-construction steps are intentionally left out of this document — the goal here is a clean, well-documented, reusable dataset.

library(data.table)
library(countrycode)

text:
Download the raw data
All source files live on the World Bank’s WITS GVC data page: https://wits.worldbank.org/gvc/gvc-data-download.html. Four files are listed there; this pipeline uses three of them:

(There is also a GVC Output zip on the same page — it is not needed for this trade-cleaning pipeline.)
Extract gvc_trade_WITS_2023.csv from the GVC Trade download and put it in the input directory alongside gvc-sectors.csv and gvc-countries.csv. The extracted trade CSV is about 6.6 GB for the release used here.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Load raw data
Three source files are needed:

dt — the raw bilateral trade / GVC flows (millions of USD)
sectors — sector code-to-group crosswalk
cty — country code reference table


raw_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_RAW_DIR", "../data/raw")
output_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_OUTPUT_DIR", "../data/temp")
dt      = fread(file.path(raw_dir, "gvc_trade_WITS_2023.csv"))
sectors = fread(file.path(raw_dir, "gvc-sectors.csv"))
cty     = fread(file.path(raw_dir, "gvc-countries.csv"))


str(dt)
head(dt)

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Classify countries into regions
We build a Region2 grouping on top of the country table:

Europe — all countries in the UN “Europe” region
ASEAN — countries in the UN “South-eastern Asia” sub-region
N.America — USA, CAN, MEX (NAFTA)
Individually tracked countries: JPN, CHN, KOR
Everything else falls into ROW (rest of world)


eurs  = codelist$iso3c[codelist$un.region.name == "Europe" &
                          !is.na(codelist$iso3c)]

asean = codelist$iso3c[codelist$un.regionsub.name == "South-eastern Asia" &
                          !is.na(codelist$iso3c)]

nafta = c("USA", "CAN", "MEX")

idvs  = c("JPN", "CHN", "KOR")

cty[, Region2 := country]
cty[country %in% eurs,  Region2 := "Europe"]
cty[country %in% asean, Region2 := "ASEAN"]
cty[country %in% nafta, Region2 := "N.America"]
cty[!country %in% c(eurs, asean, nafta, idvs), Region2 := "ROW"]


Sanity check: any countries without a region?

cty[is.na(Region2)]

If this returns rows, those countries were not matched by countrycode’s region lookup and should be assigned manually before proceeding.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: Merge trade data with sector groupings
text:
Merge trade data with sector groupings
Trade is merged onto the sector crosswalk using sect and source (the data source, e.g. wiodlr or tiva), since sector codes are not necessarily consistent across sources.

dt2 = merge(dt, sectors, by = c("sect", "source"))


Sanity check: sector coverage by source

dt2[, .N, by = .(source, sect_group)][order(source, sect_group)]

dt2[source == "wiodlr", .N, by = .(sect_group, sect_name)][order(sect_group)]

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Merge in exporter / importer regions
The region classification built above is joined twice — once for the exporter (exp) and once for the importer (imp).

dt2 = merge(dt2, cty[, .(exp = country, exp_reg = Region2)], by = "exp")
dt2 = merge(dt2, cty[, .(imp = country, imp_reg = Region2)], by = "imp")


dim(dt2)
sum(is.na(dt2$exp_reg))
sum(is.na(dt2$imp_reg))

Both NA counts should be zero after this step — any non-zero count means some exporter/importer codes in dt don’t have a match in cty and were dropped by the merge (or need to be added to the country table).

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Reshape to long format
Three sources are combined:

wiodlr for all years
tiva restricted to years after 2000
eora for 1990, 1997, 2007, and 2015

The GVC/trade-type columns (traditional_trade_int, traditional_trade_fin, gvcbp, gvcfp, gvcmix) are melted into a single variable / value pair, which is the tidy shape most of the downstream analysis expects.

dtl = melt(
  dt2[source == "wiodlr" | (source == "tiva" & t > 2000)| 
        (source=="eora" & t %in% c(1990,1997,2007,2015)),
      .(source,imp, exp, imp_reg, exp_reg,
        sect_name, sect_group,
        t, traditional_trade_int, traditional_trade_fin,
        gvcbp, gvcfp, gvcmix)],
  id.vars = c("imp", "exp",
              "imp_reg", "exp_reg",
              "sect_name", "sect_group", "t","source")
)

range(dtl$t)

The last two arguments are the input and output directories. The runner writes the cleaned files to the output directory.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
The goal of this lesson
This is not an R syntax tutorial — it’s a walkthrough of a real cleaning job: turning a messy, human-formatted Excel file into a tidy dataset ready for analysis and plotting.
The general workflow is always the same, whatever the raw data looks like:

Load the raw file, one sheet/section at a time
Inspect it — look at the actual structure before assuming anything
Clean — rename, reshape, and fix inconsistencies
Handle exceptions — real data always has special cases
Combine the cleaned pieces
Sanity-check with a quick plot before trusting the result
Save the cleaned data so the raw file is never touched again

We’ll follow that exact sequence using the Maddison Project Database (a long-run historical GDP dataset), which has two of the messiest but most common problems in real-world data: data spread across a wide, label-heavy format, and inconsistent structure between sheets.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
0. Download the raw data
Get mpd2023_web.xlsx from the Maddison Project Database on DataverseNL and place it in the input directory. To fetch the workbook from R, use the release DOI and filename shown here.
raw_file <- dataverse::get_file(
  "mpd2023_web.xlsx", dataset = "10.34894/INZBF2", server = "dataverse.nl"
)
dir.create("data/raw", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
writeBin(raw_file, file.path("data/raw", "mpd2023_web.xlsx"))

library(readxl)
library(data.table)

raw_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_RAW_DIR", "../data/raw")
output_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_OUTPUT_DIR", "../data/temp")
mdp <- file.path(raw_dir, "mpd2023_web.xlsx")







Note



Keep raw files in a data/raw/ folder and cleaned output in data/temp. Never overwrite the raw file — if a cleaning step turns out to be wrong, you want to be able to start over from the original.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
1. Load the raw data
The Maddison file has multiple sheets. We start with the “Regional data” sheet, which reports GDP per capita and population by world region.

mdp_region <- read_xlsx(mdp,
                         sheet = "Regional data",
                         skip = 1)
setDT(mdp_region)

Note skip = 1 — the first row of the sheet is a title/header banner, not column names. You only know this by opening the file and looking at it first. This is a general rule: never write cleaning code before you’ve visually inspected the raw file yourself.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
2. Inspect before cleaning

str(mdp_region)

This one str() call tells us the two problems we need to fix:

Column names are junk like ...1, ...10, ...11 — these come from Excel columns that had no header text, or a header that got interpreted as blank
Headings such as East Asia appear twice, once for GDP per capita and once for population. readxl distinguishes them with suffixes such as ...2 and ...12. The Sub-Saharan Africa columns use different spellings and need an explicit rename.

Neither of these is visible from the code alone — they only show up once you actually look at the structure of what got loaded.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
3. Clean: rename ambiguous columns

setnames(mdp_region, "...1", "date")
setnames(mdp_region, "...10", "World GDPpc")
setnames(mdp_region, "Sub Saharan Africa", "Sub Saharan Africa___1")
setnames(mdp_region, "Sub Saharan SSA", "Sub Saharan Africa___20")
mdp_region[, "...11" := NULL]

Each rename here is fixing a specific, identified problem from step 2 — not a guess. The two “Sub Saharan Africa” columns get a ___1 / ___20 suffix as a deliberate marker: it lets us split them back apart programmatically later, rather than fixing each one by hand.
mdp_region[, "...11" := NULL] drops a column that inspection showed was empty/unused — always confirm a column is genuinely unneeded before deleting it, rather than dropping anything that looks odd.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 4. Clean: reshape from wide to long
text:
4. Clean: reshape from wide to long
The workbook puts regions in separate columns. Here are two rows from the GDP-per-capita block, rounded to whole dollars.



Year
East Asia
Western Europe

The raw sheet has one column per region — wide format, convenient for a human reading a spreadsheet, but awkward for analysis. melt() converts it to long format: one row per date/region/value combination.

dt <- melt(mdp_region, id.vars = "date")

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 5. Clean: recover structure from column names
text:
5. Clean: recover structure from column names
This is the key trick in this dataset. The suffix we added in step 3 (___1, ___20) is now sitting inside the variable column, and we can split it back out into real, usable columns:

dt[, variable := gsub("\\.", "_", variable)]
dt[, c("region", "id") := tstrsplit(variable, "___")]
dt[, .N, by = id]

dt[, .N, by = id] here isn’t part of the cleaning — it’s a checkpoint. Printing a count by group after a split is a cheap way to confirm the split worked as expected before moving on.

dt[, id := as.numeric(id)]
dt[, var := ifelse(id < 10, "GDPpc", "Population")]
dt[, .N, by = .(id, var)]

The id numbers turned out to encode which variable a region’s column was (GDP per capita vs. population) — this is domain-specific knowledge you get from reading the file’s documentation or reverse-engineering the pattern, not something obvious from the code.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
6. Handle the exception case
Real datasets almost always have one row/column that doesn’t follow the general pattern. Here, the “World” totals don’t have a numeric ID suffix at all — they were named directly (“World GDPpc”, “World Population”), so the general split rule from step 5 doesn’t apply to them:

dt[variable %in% c("World GDPpc", "World Population"),
   c("region", "var") := tstrsplit(variable, " ")]
dt[, c("variable", "id") := NULL]
setnames(dt, "var", "variable")
dt[, .N, by = .(variable, region)]

Notice the pattern: apply the general rule, then explicitly patch the known exception — rather than writing one rule complex enough to cover every case at once. This keeps each step readable and debuggable.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 7. Load and clean a second sheet with different structure
text:
7. Load and clean a second sheet with different structure
Japan isn’t broken out separately in the regional sheet, so we pull it from the “Full data” sheet (which has one row per country-year) instead:

mdp_jpn <- read_xlsx(mdp, sheet = "Full data")
setDT(mdp_jpn)
str(mdp_jpn)


setnames(mdp_jpn,
         c("year", "gdppc", "pop", "country"),
         c("date", "GDPpc", "Population", "region"),
         skip_absent = TRUE)

Renaming to match the column names already used in dt (date, region) is deliberate — it’s what makes the two cleaned pieces combinable in step 8. skip_absent = TRUE means the rename won’t error if a name doesn’t exist, which is a safe default when you’re not 100% sure of every column name in a sheet you didn’t design.

dt2 <- melt(mdp_jpn[countrycode == "JPN"],
            id.vars = c("date", "region"),
            measure.vars = c("GDPpc", "Population"),
            drop = TRUE)

Same wide-to-long reshape as step 4, applied to this differently-shaped source, filtered down to just the one country we need.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
8. Combine the cleaned pieces

# Real GDP per capita in 2011$
dt3 <- rbindlist(list(dt, dt2), use.names = TRUE, fill = TRUE)

use.names = TRUE matches columns by name rather than position (safer whenever two tables were cleaned separately). fill = TRUE allows columns that exist in one piece but not the other — necessary here since dt and dt2 don’t have identical column sets.
The comment above this line matters as much as the code: always leave a note about units/definitions right next to the data, since it won’t be obvious from the column names alone months later.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
section: 9. Sanity-check with a plot before saving
text:
9. Sanity-check with a plot before saving

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(dt3[variable == "GDPpc" & date > 1900 &
             region %in% c("Japan", "East Asia", "Western Europe")],
       aes(date, value, colour = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "GDP per capita (2011 international dollars)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")




GDP per capita from the cleaned Maddison data for Japan, East Asia, and Western Europe.


This plot isn’t the final deliverable — it’s a cleaning validation step. If a region’s line looks discontinuous, jumps to an implausible value, or is missing entirely, that’s a sign of a cleaning bug, and it’s far easier to catch here than after the data has already been saved and used elsewhere.






Tip



Keep a commented-out line like this for a second variable you’re not currently checking — it costs nothing and makes it trivial to re-check later:
# ggpubr::ggline(dt3[variable=="Population"&date>1900],
#                x="date",y="value",color="region",
#                numeric.x.axis = T)

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
10. Save the cleaned data

fwrite(dt3[!is.na(value)], file.path(output_dir, "madison.csv"))

Two decisions worth calling out:

dt3[!is.na(value)] drops rows with no value at the save step, not earlier — keeping NA rows around during cleaning makes it easier to spot where gaps came from, but there’s no reason to ship them in the final file
Saving to .csv in a data/ (not data.raw/) folder means anything downstream (a graphing script, another student, future-you) never needs to re-open the original Excel file or re-run this cleaning again

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
11. Build a companion lookup table
Not every useful output has to be the main dataset. Here we also save a small reference table mapping country codes to regions, which other scripts can join against later:

mdp <- read_xlsx(mdp, sheet = "Full data")
setDT(mdp)
regions <- unique(mdp[, .(countrycode, country, region)])
regions[, .N, by = region]
regions[grepl("Western Offshoots", region), .N, by = country]
fwrite(regions, file.path(output_dir, "madison_regions.csv"))

The two .N checks here are, again, checkpoints — confirming the region grouping looks sensible (right number of regions, right countries inside a given region) before trusting the lookup table enough to save it.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Summary: the general pattern








Step
What
Why




Load
read_xlsx() one sheet at a time
Different sheets often have different structure


Inspect
str()
Reveals problems (bad names, duplicates) invisible in code alone


Rename
setnames()
Fix ambiguous/duplicate names before reshaping


Reshape
melt()
Wide (human-readable) → long (analysis-ready)


Recover structure
tstrsplit() on encoded names
Turn a naming trick back into real columns


Handle exceptions
Targeted dt[condition, ...] fix
Apply general rule, then patch known special cases


Combine
rbindlist(..., fill = TRUE)
Merge cleaned pieces from different sources


Validate
Quick plot or .N by group
Catch cleaning bugs before they reach saved data


Save
fwrite() to a separate data/ folder
Never re-touch the raw file; downstream work reads the clean version



This same sequence applies to almost any messy raw dataset — the details of what’s messy change, but the order of operations doesn’t.

title: Japanese outward FDI: ASEAN destinations and industries, 2024
text:
Japanese outward FDI: ASEAN destinations and industries, 2024
Source: Ministry of Finance, Outward / Inward Direct Investment, breakdown by Region and Industry (Annual totals), 2024 calendar year.

Published table: https://www.mof.go.jp/policy/international_policy/reference/balance_of_payments/revised/bprfdi20240112.pdf
Excel: https://www.mof.go.jp/policy/international_policy/reference/balance_of_payments/revised/fdi2024.xlsx
Index: https://www.mof.go.jp/english/policy/international_policy/reference/balance_of_payments/ebpfdii.htm

The CSV transcribes the published numeric table inspected on 2026-11-18. Page numbers are one-based: page 1 contains regional/industry totals and page 3 contains the six ASEAN destination economies shown on the slide.
The comparison was extended to selected major destinations outside ASEAN: China (page 3), India (page 4), United States (page 5), Australia (page 7), and United Kingdom, Netherlands and Germany (page 8). It is a selected comparison, not an exhaustive ranking of the world’s largest recipients. Singapore is included in both the worldwide comparison and the detailed ASEAN chart.
Values are annual net outward FDI flows, in 100 million yen. Divide by 10 for billions of yen. They are compiled on the directional principle, not the asset/liability principle of the headline balance-of-payments series. Do not mix their denominators with the existing MOF financial-account charts.
Non-manufacturing includes service industries but also agriculture, mining, construction and other industries; it is not synonymous with services. The four selected service industries are components of non-manufacturing and must not be added to its total. The source’s narrow category “Services” is not a total for all service industries and is deliberately not used as such.
Source totals may differ slightly from the sum of rounded components. Use the published Total rows for regional shares and displayed totals. The chart shows six selected ASEAN economies; the ASEAN aggregate also includes other members covered by the source. The source’s country classification for 2024 is retained.

title: Vietnam FDI, ODA and gross fixed capital formation, 1991-2019
text:
Compiled on 2026-11-18 to investigate slides/image/vietnam_fdi_oda.png. The CSV is transcribed from the published numeric tables below, not digitized from the image. It is a candidate reconstruction dataset, not a verified copy of the image author’s original workbook.
All amount columns are in millions of current US dollars. Percentage columns are calculated as 100 times the amount divided by GFCF. Blank values mean unavailable, not zero. GFCF is missing for 1991-1993 in the archived table, so the corresponding shares are left blank, consistent with the image’s lines starting in 1994.



Column: fdi_implemented_usd_million.
Measure: implemented/realized FDI capital in Vietnam, not registered capital and not the World Bank balance-of-payments net inflow series.
Transcription source: https://www.jpvn.org/statst-j/VN-fdi-statistics-1988-2024.html
That table cites Vietnam’s Statistical Yearbook 2022, Table 131 and NSO PXWeb.
Official corroboration of 2019’s USD 20.38 billion: https://www.mpi.gov.vn/en/Pages/2020/Brief-on-foreign-direct-investment-of-2019-176349.aspx
Another official yearbook source: https://www.nso.gov.vn/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/NG-TCTK-2023_Final.pdf





Column: net_oda_received_usd_million.
Measure: net ODA received by Vietnam from all donors, not Japan alone.
Indicator: DT.ODA.ODAT.CD.
Transcription source (archived World Bank/OECD series reproduced by IndexMundi): https://www.indexmundi.com/facts/vietnam/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.CD
Primary indicator page: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/DT.ODA.ODAT.CD





Column: gfcf_usd_million.
Measure: gross fixed capital formation, current US dollars.
Indicator: NE.GDI.FTOT.CD.
Transcription source (archived World Bank series reproduced by IndexMundi): https://www.indexmundi.com/facts/vietnam/indicator/NE.GDI.FTOT.CD
Primary indicator page: https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/NE.GDI.FTOT.CD




The archived values are used deliberately because they appear consistent with the graph. Current releases differ in some years. For example, the archived 2019 GFCF is USD 63,469.790 million, giving FDI/GFCF of 32.1098% and ODA/GFCF of 1.7247%. The image visually shows approximately 32% and 2%, respectively. The archived 1994 values give approximately 56.69% and 22.66%, also consistent with the start of the image’s lines. These checks support the reconstruction but do not establish the original data vintage or source for every point.
The underlying flows have different statistical definitions; the calculated ratios compare their magnitudes and are not additive national-accounts shares.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
This page shows the R code and sample results. To regenerate the full dataset, run the following from the repository root with PWT_GA.csv available.
The last two arguments are the input and output directories. The runner writes the cleaned files to the output directory.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Download the data
Export the Growth Accounting (GA) table from the Penn World Table data tool. Select the countries and years you need, then save the CSV as PWT_GA.csv in the input directory. The local export used for the example covers 1950–2019 and reports real GDP at constant 2017 national prices.

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Load data

library(data.table)

raw_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_RAW_DIR", "../data/raw")
output_dir <- Sys.getenv("JWE_OUTPUT_DIR", "../data/temp")
pwt <- file.path(raw_dir, "PWT_GA.csv")

pwtd = fread(pwt, header = T)
setnames(pwtd, gsub(" ", "", colnames(pwtd)))
str(pwtd)
pwtd[, .N, by = .(Variablecode, Variablename)]

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:
Reshape to long format

pwtdl = melt(pwtd,
             id.vars = c("Variablecode", "Variablename",
                         "ISOcode", "Country"),
             variable.name = "date",
             variable.factor = FALSE)

setorder(pwtdl, ISOcode, Variablename, date)

title: Cleaning Raw Data: A Worked Example
text:

pwtdl[, Lvalue := shift(value, type = "lag"),
      by = .(ISOcode, Variablename)]

pwtdl[, date := as.numeric(date)]

pwtdl[, Variablename2 := trimws(gsub("(\\(|\\,|by\\b|at\\b).*$", "",
                                      Variablename))]

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Why countries trade?

Comparative advantage: difference in resources or productivity
Economic of scales: similar countries trade if production get cheaper at larger scale

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Absolute vs. Comparative advantage

Being better at producing everything is absolute advantage: does not determine what gets traded.
Comparative advantage is about relative opportunity cost: what you give up to produce more unit of something.
Even a country with no absolute advantage in anything still has a comparative advantage in something.

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Explaining Japan’s trade patterns

Productivity/technology differences
Short-run immobility
Capital vs. labor abundance

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Productivity differences

Core idea: countries export the good where their opportunity cost is lowest.
Japan’s technology edge in precision manufacturing lowers the opportunity cost of producing autos and electronics relative to its trading partners.
In agriculture, Japan has higher opportunity costs, which driving the import patterns

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Short-run immobility

Core idea: some factors (land, sector-specific capital) can’t quickly move between industries.
Japan’s farmland and farmers can’t retrain into auto manufacturing overnight.
Despite comparative disadvantage in agriculture, Japan has long-standing protection policy.

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Factor abundance

Core idea: countries export goods that intensively use their abundance factor.
Japan is capital- and technology-abundant relative to land and labor.
Japan export capital-intensive goods (car, electronics) and imports land/labor-intensive goods (food, raw materials)

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Which lens fits Japan best?

Exports where relative productivity is highest
Protection of agriculture despite comparative disadvantage
Exports capital-intensive goods, imports land/labor-intensive goods

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan

What drives comparative advantage?

Kowalski (2011, OECD): 55 OECD and emerging economies.


Convergence across countries

Physical capital
Education (tertiary, avg. schooling)
Primary energy supply
Financial development (credit)


Divergence across countries

Secondary education

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Convergence differs by trade relationship

North-North (within OECD): became more homogeneous on most sources
South-South (within non-OECD): gap remains for capital-to-labor ratio and regulatory indicators but narrowed for education, energy supply, financial development.
North-South (OECD vs. non-OECD): Gap widened for physical capital, credit availability, regulatory quality but narrowed for human capital

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Revealed comparative advantages
The Balassa index (Balassa, 1965): how much more (or less) a country exports of a good, relative to its share of world trade.
\[
RCA = \frac{\text{country's export share of good X}}
{\text{world's export share of good X}}
\]

RCA > 1: the country exports proportionally more of that good than the world average



effective only within same country among products or same product among countries: higher value indicates a stronger export performance, higher degree of export specialization, and a higher degree of revealed comparative advantage

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
RCA of Japan across period



1965–1974: RCA concentrated in labor-intensive, lower-technology sectors – Highest: Textiles, Textile, Leather and Footwear – Also elevated: Basic Metals and Fabricated Metal; Machinery, nec.
1975–1984: Transition period – Textiles RCA begins declining – Transport Equipment, Machinery, and Electrical/Optical Equipment start rising
1985–2000: RCA concentrated in capital- and technology-intensive sectors – Highest: Transport Equipment; Electrical and Optical Equipment; Machinery, nec. – Textiles falls to the bottom of the distribution

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
section: Limits of RCA as a measure
text:
Limits of RCA as a measure

RCA reflects actual trade flows, which are already shaped by tariffs, subsidies, and protection, not a “pure” underlying advantage.
Global value chains: a “Japanese” car may contain parts made in many countries, blurring what RCA is really measuring.
Categorization-sensitive: results can shift depending on how narrowly or broadly a “sector” is defined.

title: Comparative Advantage: The case of Japan
text:
Key takeaways

Japan’s trade pattern can be explained by theories on comparative advantages.
RCA gives us an empirical way to confirm the pattern the theories predict.
RCA has its limits

Japan tariff

Source: WTO Tariff Profile (2025)
Tariff line: the most detailed product category in a country’s tariff schedule, identified by a national code (usually 8 to 10 digits, built on the 6-digit HS code). Each tariff line has its own duty rate. “AVG”, “Duty-free in %”, “Max” and “Binding in %” are all calculated over tariff lines, not over trade value.

Final bound duties: the maximum tariff rates Japan has committed to the WTO for each product line. Japan cannot legally raise tariffs above these ceilings.
MFN applied duties: the rates Japan actually charges other WTO members under the Most-Favoured-Nation principle, i.e. the non-discriminatory “normal” tariff, excluding preferential rates under FTAs. Applied rates are at or below bound rates.
AVG: simple average of the ad valorem tariff rates (%) across all lines in the group.
Duty-free in %: share of tariff lines with a zero rate.
Max: the highest single tariff rate in the group (italics mark non-ad valorem rates converted to ad valorem equivalents).
Binding in %: share of tariff lines that are bound at the WTO (100 means every line is bound).
Imports (Share in %): the group’s share of Japan’s total imports.
Imports (Duty-free in %): share of the group’s import value that enters duty-free.

title: Foreign Direct Investment
text:
Key concepts: FDI, M&A, MNEs

FDI: cross-border investment with a lasting interest and control (commonly a 10% voting-share threshold)

Forms: greenfield, M&A, reinvested earnings

M&A: acquiring or merging with an existing foreign firm, rather than building new capacity
MNEs: firms that own and control operations in more than one country; the main actors behind FDI
Motives: market-seeking, resource-seeking, efficiency-seeking

title: Foreign Direct Investment
text:
FDI vs. portfolio investment

Direct investment: lasting interest and influence over management of a foreign enterprise (typically 10% or more of voting power).
Portfolio investment: cross-border holdings of securities without a direct-investment relationship.
Direct investment is closely linked to multinational production and global value chains; portfolio flows are generally more liquid and volatile.



In the balance of payments, both direct and portfolio investment are recorded in the financial account.
The Balance of Payments lecture shows that Japan’s portfolio flows have been more volatile than direct investment flows.

title: Foreign Direct Investment
section: Why do countries want inward FDI?
text:
Why do countries want inward FDI?


Capital: finance factories, equipment, and business expansion.
Jobs and income: create employment and demand for domestic suppliers.
Technology and skills: introduce production methods, management practices, and worker training.
Export opportunities: connect domestic production to multinational firms’ international networks.
Productivity and growth: domestic firms may benefit through learning and supplier relationships.

Benefits are not automatic: local skills and firms’ ability to absorb technology matter.



Borensztein, De Gregorio, and Lee (1998) emphasize the role of human capital in realizing growth benefits from FDI: https://www.nber.org/papers/w5057
Javorcik (2004) finds evidence consistent with productivity spillovers to domestic suppliers in Lithuania: https://www.aeaweb.org/articles?id=10.1257/0002828041464605

title: Foreign Direct Investment
text:
Complementary vs. Substitution

Complementary view:

ODA builds preconditions for private investment (infrastructure, governance).
Especially in low-income countries where private capital avoids risk.

Substitution view:

Excessive aid can crowd out FDI if it distorts markets or maintains uncompetitive sectors.
Conditional or tied aid may limit spillovers.

title: Foreign Direct Investment

Japan’s Experience


Tied aid and “ingredients approach” → enabled Japanese firms to invest later.

Transition from aid-recipient to investment-partner relationship.

title: Foreign Direct Investment
text:
Discussions


Is it a problem that Japan’s outward FDI is about six times its inward FDI? Yes, no, or it depends?
Japan removed most legal restrictions on inward FDI decades ago, but inward FDI is still low. Looking at the METI survey table, which barrier could the government actually fix, and which could it not?
Private investors avoid risky, low-return countries, but ODA goes there. How could ODA make a country like Vietnam more attractive to private investors?
Japan’s tied aid helped Japanese firms invest later. Is that good development cooperation or aid serving the donor’s interests?

title: Exchange Rate and Competitiveness
text:
Purchasing power parity (PPP)

\[ q_t = S_t \times \frac{P_{US,t}}{P_{JP,t}} \]

\(S_t\): nominal exchange rate, yen per dollar (USD/JPY)
\(q_t\): price of US goods relative to Japanese goods, both in yen
Absolute PPP: \(q = 1\). The same basket costs the same in both countries.
Relative PPP: \(q\) stays constant as changes in \(S\) offset the inflation gap.
A higher \(q\) means a weaker yen in real terms and cheaper Japanese goods relative to US goods.




To express the real exchange rate as an index, divide \(q_t\) by its base-year value and multiply by 100. In the apple example, \(q = 1\) in the base year, so the index starts at 100.
